 2   Q6.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

 3   A.    The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to the direct testimonies filed

 4         by: City of Las Cruces (“CLC”) witness Ted Thomas, the Utility Division Staff

 5         (“Staff”) of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“NMPRC”)

 6         witnesses Douglas Jester and Orland Whitney, Walmart Inc. (“Walmart”) witness

11         updated rebuttal allocation factors, the treatment of distributed solar generation

12         customers in the distribution allocator, the proposed hourly allocation model

16   Q7.   STAFF WITNESS JESTER CONCLUDES THAT THE USE OF SAMPLING

17         MAY BE MATERIALLY OVERSTATING DEMAND STATISTICS FOR

18         RESIDENTIAL           CUSTOMERS           AND    UNDERSTATING          DEMAND

19         STATISTICS FOR OTHER CLASSES. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR.

20         JESTER’S ASSESMENT?

 1   A.    No. As stated in my direct testimony, because the advanced metering system

 2         (“AMS”) rollout was not completed at the start of the Base Period, there may be

 3         some inherited bias in the population estimates shown in Exhibit ES-1 of my direct

 4         testimony. The existence of differences between the sampled and population

 5         studies are expected and do not, on their own, demonstrate that the sampling

 6         resulted in overstating residential demand statistics while understating demand

 7         statistics for other classes. In fact, the graphs in Exhibit ES-1 show that the results

10   Q8.   ARE THERE ANY CONCERNS ABOUT MR. JESTER’S ANALYSIS

11         COMPARING POPULATION AND SAMPLED STUDIES?

12   A.    Yes. Although EPE used all AMS data available at the time the studies were

13         developed, a portion of active residential customers were not represented in the

14         population study at the end of the Base Period, and the population study included

15         fewer customers earlier in the Base Period. Therefore, the study does not represent

16         a complete census for the residential customer population.

17                This limitation is important when interpreting Mr. Jester’s comparison.

18         Because the load characteristics of the customers without complete AMS data are

19         unknown, it cannot be assumed that the population estimates are necessarily more

20         accurate than the sampled estimates. Accordingly, differences between the two

 2   Q10. HOW DO THE SAMPLE AND POPULATION RESULTS COMPARE

 3              WHEN APPLIED TO THE WAY EPE DEVELOPS ITS ALLOCATION

 4              FACTORS?

 5   A.         As explained in my direct testimony, class maximum and coincident demands are

 6              determined by applying the load and coincidence factors from the load studies to

 7              billed energy. What matters for allocation is the relationship between demand and

 8              energy in each month, not the level of energy or demand per customer. When the

 9              sample’s monthly ratio of coincident demand to energy is applied to the

10              population’s energy, the resulting 4CP demand is within 4 percent of the

11              population-based 4CP demand for every sampled class: 101.2 percent for Rate 01,

12              96.0 percent for Rate 03, 98.1 percent for Rate 04, 99.4 percent for Rate 05, 97.0

13              percent for Rate 07, and 102.6 percent for Rate 08. For the residential class, the

14              difference is approximately 1 percent. These differences are within the plus or

15              minus 10 percent precision at 90 percent confidence that the AEIC Load Research

16              Manual identifies as the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act guideline for load

17              research at the time of class and system peaks. 2

10   Q12. IS         SAMPLING           A    PROVEN           AND   ACCEPTED     METHOD        FOR

11              ESTIMATING AVERAGES FOR A LARGE POPULATION?

12   A.         Yes. Statistical sampling is a well-established method for estimating characteristics

13              of a larger population from a properly designed sample. Sampling methods are

14              used across a broad range of fields. In the electric industry, the AIEC Load

15              Research Manual specifically recognizes sampling as an appropriate method for

16              estimating customer-class load characteristics.

17

18   Q13. ARE THERE ANY CONCERNS WITH USING POPULATION STUDIES IN

19              THIS RATE CASE OR IN FUTURE RATE CASES?

 1   A.   Yes. As discussed in my direct testimony, there are several considerations

 2        associated with the use of population studies. For the Base Period in this case, the

 3        AMS rollout had not yet been completed, and AMS meters were installed

 4        geographically over time. As a result, the available AMS population may contain

 5        geographic bias.

 6                Although the AMS rollout is now complete, population studies will still

 7        exclude customers who declined AMS metering, this can also cause some bias.

 8                There are also practical considerations. Analyzing the entire population is

 9        more resource intensive in terms of data processing, computing requirements and

10        analyst review. The larger volume of data can make it more difficult to perform

11        the same level of detailed validation and review for every customer. By contrast, a

12        properly designed sample can allow for more intensive review of the underlying

13        data while still producing statistically reliable estimates of population

14        characteristics.

17        OF    SAMPLE       VERSUS      POPULATION          DATA      IN   EPE’S     LOAD

20        research results based on samples for this case and that the Commission should

 3   Q15. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. JESTER’S RECOMMENDATION?

 4   A.   Partially. While I do agree that the Commission should accept the sampled studies

 5        for this case, I do not agree that the Commission should direct EPE’s load research

 6        to use population-based studies only for future cases. While population-based

 7        studies may be the correct solution for the smaller rate classes, it may not be the

 8        best solution for larger rate classes such as residential.

 9

10   Q16. HOW DOES EPE PLAN TO LEVERAGE AMS DATA IN FUTURE RATE

11        CASES?

12   A.   EPE anticipates using a population-based approach, particularly for rate classes

13        with a relatively small number of customers for which complete AMS data are

14        available. For larger rate classes, such as the residential class, EPE anticipates

15        using significantly larger samples, or “super samples,” rather than including every

16        customer in the population. This will allow EPE to take advantage of the substantial

17        amount of information available through AMS while maintaining appropriate data

18        validation and quality-control procedures.       EPE will evaluate the appropriate

19        methodology and sample size for each rate class. EPE does not anticipate applying

20        a single methodology across all rate classes.          Instead, EPE intends to use



                                                 9

                                      ENEDINA SOTO


 1        population-based studies where practical and representative super samples for

 2        classes with substantially larger customer populations.

 4   Q41. HOW IS THE LOAD FACTOR USED IN THE AVERAGE & EXCESS

 5        (“A&E”) ALLOCATION FACTOR CALCULATION?

 6   A.   The A&E calculation is made up of two components, the average demand/energy

 7        component and the excess demand component. The average demand represents the

 8        average energy use across all hours of the year, while the excess demand

 9        component represents the demand above average usage. The resulting allocation

10        factor is the weighted average proportion of both of these components for each

11        class. The energy component is weighted using the load factor, while the excess

12        demand component is weighted by 1-Load Factor. The importance of the load

13        factor is that it determines how much weight is given to the energy component of

14        the A&E calculation.

17        WEIGHTING FACTOR IN EPE’S 4CP A&E ALLOCATOR?

18   A.   The system load factor is an appropriate weighting factor because it reflects the

19        relationship between the system’s average demand and peak demand and is

20        therefore consistent with cost-causation principles. Under the A&E methodology,

 3        excess-demand component.

 6        component and less weight on excess demand. Conversely, a lower system load

 7        factor indicates a greater difference between average and peak demand and

 8        therefore places greater weight on the excess-demand component. This approach

 9        appropriately recognizes that customers or rate classes whose demands contribute

10        more significantly to the system’s capacity requirements should be allocated a

11        greater share of those capacity-related costs.
